title: Last Chance Harvey
full_review:
The delicate romantic comedy "Last Chance Harvey" (Overture) chronicles the budding relationship between two isolated middle-age characters -- one long divorced, the other never married -- who meet in a chance encounter at London's Heathrow Airport.

British survey-taker Kate (Emma Thompson) has the unenviable task of quizzing arriving passengers about their journey. Many of them are exhausted and disposed to be rude, and indeed she gets short shrift when she approaches New York jingle composer Harvey Shine (Dustin Hoffman) who has hopped the pond to attend the wedding of his estranged daughter, Susan (Liane Balaban).

Harvey is suffering considerable anxiety over his professional future, since his boss, Marvin (Richard Schiff) -- convinced Harvey is losing favor with their clients -- has just warned him that there are to be "no more chances." Harvey also is less than enthused at the prospect of seeing his ex, Jean (Kathy Baker), now happily remarried to dapper, gregarious Brian (James Brolin).

By the time Kate and Harvey cross paths again in an airport bar, Harvey has embarrassed himself at the rehearsal dinner, missed his return flight and been summarily fired. He also has been devastated by the fact that Susan chose to have Brian give her away.

Kate, meanwhile, has gone on a disappointing blind date and been dogged by repeated cell phone calls from her fretful mother, Maggie (Eileen Atkins), who suspects that her Polish neighbor (Robert Jezek) is doing something nefarious.

As Kate takes solace in a paperback novel and a glass of chardonnay, Harvey uses the opportunity to apologize, and the two are soon exchanging gentle jibes. With nothing to lose and nowhere to go before the next day's flight, Harvey follows her into town.

Teasing gives way to spontaneous confidences as the two stroll the capital's streets and quays, and Kate urges Harvey, who has confessed his sense of failure as a father, to take advantage of his altered itinerary by attending Susan's reception.

While somewhat predictable, writer-director Joel Hopkins' skillfully wrought valentine to midlife romance draws masterful performances from stars at the top of their game and an impressive supporting cast. As it portrays a mutually generous relationship untainted by irresponsible sexuality, his script also shows the lingering negative consequences of both divorce and abortion.

The film contains some sexual references and humor, occasional crude words, the acceptability of divorce and an abortion reference. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
